sections.text: To find how many tiles you need, divide the room area by the area of one tile, round up, then add a waste allowance for cuts and breakage. For a 12 ft by 10 ft room (120 square feet) tiled with 12 in by 24 in tiles, each tile covers 2 square feet, so you need 60 tiles. Adding a 10 percent allowance gives 66 tiles, which is 7 boxes if a box holds 10 tiles. The waste percentage changes with the layout pattern, and that is where most ordering mistakes happen.

items: Room area in square feet = length x width. Here 12 x 10 = 120.
Tile area in square feet = (tile length in inches x tile width in inches) / 144. Here (12 x 24) / 144 = 2.
Base tile count = room area / tile area, rounded up. Here 120 / 2 = 60.
Total tiles = base count x (1 + waste percentage), rounded up. Here 60 x 1.10 = 66.
Boxes = total tiles / tiles per box, rounded up. Here 66 / 10 = 6.6, so 7 boxes.

sections.text: The Tile Calculator uses exactly this method with fixed layout allowances: 10 percent for a standard grid or brick pattern, 15 percent for diagonal and 20 percent for herringbone. You can override the percentage if your installer recommends a different figure. It also assumes 10 tiles per box, which may not match your product, so always check the tiles per box and square feet per box printed on the carton.

The table below uses the same 12 ft by 10 ft room with 12 in by 24 in tiles. Only the layout changes. The cost column assumes an illustrative price of 3.50 dollars per tile, which is a placeholder and not a market price.

Notice what the numbers say. Going from a grid to herringbone adds 6 tiles, or 21 dollars at the assumed price. The tile itself is a small part of the risk. The bigger costs are the extra cutting time and the chance of running short and finding that the next lot does not match.
Tile size changes both the count and how coarse the waste allowance is. The table uses the same 120 square foot room with a 10 percent grid allowance.

With large-format tile, 10 percent rounds up to just 2 spare pieces, and each piece is 8 square feet. A single miscut or a tile that arrives chipped uses up half of your cushion. For large-format tile or very small rooms it can be sensible to plan more than the standard percentage. Ask your installer rather than relying on a single rule.
Do grout lines change the count?

Slightly. Each tile plus its grout joint occupies a little more than the tile alone, so you need marginally fewer tiles. Assuming a 1/8 in joint and the nominal tile sizes, the raw count in 120 square feet falls as follows:

The Tile Calculator accepts a grout width but does not subtract it from the tile count, so its answer is slightly conservative. The reduction is smaller than the waste allowance, so most people ignore it. Wider joints, rectified edges and actual versus nominal tile sizes all shift the numbers a little, so use the sizes printed on the box.

items: Entering the tile size in feet when the calculator expects inches, or the reverse. Always confirm the unit label.
Ordering exactly the base count with no waste. Every edge tile needs a cut, and some cuts fail.
Treating a box as the unit of purchase without checking its coverage. Boxes are sold by tile count or by square feet, and the two differ between products.
Ignoring rooms that are not rectangles. For an L-shaped room, add the areas of the two sections first (for example 168 square feet for a 12 x 10 plus a 6 x 8), then apply the allowance once.
Not keeping spare tile. Product lines get discontinued and dye lots vary, so leftover boxes are your repair supply.

sections.text: When this method does not apply

The calculation assumes a flat, rectangular floor covered edge to edge. It does not model walls, backsplashes, stair risers, patterned tile that must be matched, or trim pieces such as bullnose edging, which you count separately by length. Substrate preparation, tile adhesive and grout quantities depend on the manufacturer instructions, and wet areas may be governed by local building codes. Confirm the layout and the product requirements with the manufacturer or a licensed installer before you order.
Lay out a dry run of a few rows before you spread any adhesive. It shows you where the cuts will fall and whether you need to shift the starting line so edge tiles are not slivers.

sections.heading: Starting a tiling project?
sections.body: Use the Tile Calculator to get the exact number of tiles and boxes you need. It supports grid, brick, diagonal, and herringbone layouts with automatic waste factors.
